title: Explainer: How sea level rise poses an ‘existential threat’ to humans, heritage and nature - Carbon Brief
gist: Oceans are rising faster than at any point in at least three millennia, already putting 770 million people, major coastal cities, coral reefs, low-lying island nations and hundreds of UNESCO heritage sites at escalating risk, with existing sea walls and adaptation measures projected to fail far more often within decades under even moderate-emissions scenarios.

themes.theme: Pace and scale of sea level rise

insights.claim: Global sea levels are rising faster than at any time in at least the past three millennia, and human influence has been the dominant cause of sea level rise since at least 1970.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Confirms sea level rise as an accelerating, human-caused, non-reversible-on-short-timescales risk factor for coastal infrastructure, insurance and real estate valuations globally.
insights.quote: The world’s oceans are currently rising at a faster rate than at any time in at least the past three millennia, with human influence the “dominant cause” of sea level rise since at least 1970.
insights.locator: Opening paragraphs

insights.claim: Global average sea level rose 20cm between 1901 and 2018, but the pace has accelerated sharply, with 10.6cm of that rise occurring just since 1993.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: More than half of a century's worth of sea level rise has occurred in the last ~30 years, signaling the risk curve is steepening, not linear — relevant for long-duration infrastructure and coastal asset planning.
insights.locator: On average, global sea levels rose by 20 centimetres

insights.claim: Under a moderate-emissions scenario, scientists project global average sea level will rise an additional 56cm by 2100 relative to a 1995-2014 baseline.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A ~56cm baseline rise this century is the planning benchmark investors in coastal infrastructure, ports, and property should use for moderate-case exposure modeling.
insights.locator: Under a moderate-emissions scenario, scientists predict

insights.claim: The frequency of 100-year 'extreme sea level events' — where high tides, storm surges and relative sea level rise combine — has already increased 12-fold since 1900, and under a moderate-emissions scenario these events are likely to occur at least annually in many places by end of century.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Formerly rare 'once-a-century' coastal flood events becoming annual occurrences implies a step-change in insured losses and reinsurance pricing for coastal property.
insights.locator: The frequency of 100-year “extreme sea level events”

insights.claim: Around 770 million people — 10% of the world's population — are at 'acute risk' from sea level rise, defined as living in locations less than five metres above the high-tide line, including residents of Mumbai, Kolkata, Shenzhen and Guangzhou and the entire populations of many island nations.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Names specific megacities with large economic bases (Shenzhen, Guangzhou are major manufacturing/tech hubs) as acute-risk zones — a direct link between sea level rise and Asian industrial/economic exposure.
insights.locator: Around 770 million people

insights.claim: Even without any future sea level rise, global flood losses in the world's 136 largest coastal cities could reach up to $52bn per year by 2050, up from $6bn in 2005, driven mainly by continued coastal development.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: An ~8-9x increase in baseline urban flood losses by 2050 (even isolating out further sea rise) is a quantifiable, investable trend for insurers, reinsurers and municipal infrastructure spend.
insights.locator: The associated development of coastal areas

insights.claim: Population living within 5km of a coast grew 28% between 2000 and 2018, outpacing the 23% global population growth rate over the same period, meaning coastal exposure is increasing even as risk rises.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Structural mismatch: people keep concentrating in the riskiest zones faster than population grows overall, compounding future loss potential independent of climate trajectory.
insights.locator: But even as the risks from sea level rise increase

insights.claim: Jakarta, Indonesia has been sinking by up to 15cm per year over the past decade, largely due to groundwater overextraction causing aquifer collapse — a local subsidence rate that can equal or exceed climate-driven sea level rise.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Illustrates that local land subsidence from groundwater extraction can be a far larger and faster driver of relative sea level rise than global climate trends — a distinct, manageable risk factor for water-stressed megacities.
insights.locator: One notable example is Jakarta

insights.claim: Venice's MOSE flood-barrier system, engaged for the first time in October 2020, was activated 48 more times in the following two years, showing rapidly increasing deployment frequency of major engineered coastal defenses.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A concrete case study of large-scale coastal defense capex (MOSE) and its rising activation cadence — relevant precedent for capital-intensive flood infrastructure spend elsewhere.
insights.locator: In 2003, the Italian city of Venice

insights.claim: Under a low-emissions scenario, existing coastal flood protections may be breached 10 times as frequently over the next 30 years as they currently are.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Even in the best-case emissions pathway, current infrastructure is expected to become an order of magnitude less protective — implying continuous, rising capex need for coastal defense upgrades regardless of climate policy success.
insights.locator: However, existing adaptations may not be sufficient

insights.claim: 'Coastal squeeze' — where ecosystems trying to migrate inland due to sea level rise are blocked by human development — has contributed to the loss of nearly 28m hectares of coastal wetlands (an area roughly the size of Ecuador) since 1970.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A named mechanism (coastal squeeze) for a large, quantified habitat loss — relevant to natural-capital/ESG risk assessment and to carbon-sequestration capacity loss from wetland destruction.
insights.quote: Coastal squeeze has contributed to the widespread loss of the world’s wetlands.
insights.locator: This combination of pressures is called “coastal squeeze”

insights.claim: In the continental US, only 16% of coastal wetlands are migrating inland fast enough to outpace local sea level rise, while 11% are submerging outright.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A specific, measurable adaptation failure rate (84% not keeping pace) for US wetlands useful for natural-capital risk models tied to US coastal real estate and conservation investment.
insights.locator: In the continental US, just 16%

insights.claim: A 2013 study modeling one metre of sea level rise across 10 island biodiversity hotspots (nearly 4,450 islands) found ~6% of island habitat area would be completely submerged and over 11% of hotspot islands would lose at least half their land area, putting dozens of species at extinction risk.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Quantifies biodiversity-hotspot vulnerability to a specific, plausible sea-rise scenario — relevant to conservation-linked finance and biodiversity credit markets.
insights.locator: A 2013 study modelled the impact

insights.claim: In 2024, researchers documented the first known local extinction (extirpation) of a US plant species due to sea level rise: the Key Largo cactus, killed off by hurricanes, storm surge, soil erosion and saltwater intrusion, with the last specimens removed in 2021 for greenhouse cultivation.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated first-of-its-kind biodiversity casualty attributable to sea level rise — a marker event for tracking accelerating ecological impact in the US.
insights.locator: In 2024, researchers documented the first known extirpation

themes.theme: Small island developing states existential exposure

insights.claim: Sea level rise poses an 'acute and disproportionate' threat to small island developing states because many Pacific atolls have average elevations of just 1-2 metres and maximum elevations of only 3-5 metres above sea level.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Frames entire nations as existentially exposed within decades, not centuries — relevant to sovereign risk, climate migration flows, and geopolitical realignment in the Pacific.
insights.quote: Even under moderate scenarios, rising seas will render many low-lying coastal zones and small island developing states increasingly uninhabitable without extraordinary adaptation.
insights.locator: Sea level rise poses an “acute and disproportionate” threat

insights.claim: Most Pacific small island nations sit in a region where relative sea level rise from Antarctic ice sheet melt is projected to be 11-33% higher than the global average by 2100, regardless of emissions scenario.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A geophysical gravitational/ocean-circulation effect means Pacific islands face above-average sea rise essentially independent of future emissions policy — an unavoidable, locked-in regional risk.
insights.locator: In addition, most of the small-island nations

insights.claim: Kiribati lost two small uninhabited islands to rising seas in 1999, and by 2014 several uninhabited Solomon Islands had vanished with six more severely eroded, forcing relocation of some communities.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Documented island disappearance is not hypothetical — it has already happened multiple times, establishing a track record for forecasting further losses.
insights.locator: In 1999, Kiribati lost two small

insights.claim: Small island developing states need up to $6bn annually by 2035 to adapt to climate change but received just $1.2bn in public adaptation finance in 2022-23 — roughly a fifth of stated need.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A large, quantified and persistent adaptation-finance gap for a defined group of vulnerable sovereigns — a target market for climate adaptation funds, green bonds and multilateral finance vehicles.
insights.locator: According to the UN, these countries will require up to $6bn

insights.claim: Small island developing states currently face $1.64bn in expected annual climate damages from coastal flooding (0.13% of cumulative GDP), but this is projected to grow to $24bn per year even if warming is limited to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A roughly 15x jump in projected annual damages even under the most optimistic 1.5C warming pathway underscores that mitigation alone won't spare these economies — adaptation finance is non-optional.
insights.locator: Currently, small island developing states experience

insights.claim: A 2025 UN International Law Commission report concluded international law allows countries' maritime borders to stay fixed even as coastlines change due to sea level rise, while calling for new legal frameworks to protect displaced persons.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Resolves a major legal uncertainty (loss of exclusive economic zones as islands submerge) in favor of vulnerable island states — protects their fishing/resource rights even if landmass disappears, a material outcome for sovereign economic interests.
insights.quote: There is a need to develop legal and practical solutions to better protect persons affected by sea level rise, including those who remain in situ and those who are internally or externally displaced by it.
insights.locator: However, a 2025 report by the UN International Law Commission

insights.claim: Sea level rise has a dual effect on coral reefs: deeper water can buffer reefs against marine heatwaves and ocean warming, but it also reduces light penetration needed for coral survival, while associated erosion adds sediment that impedes coral feeding, reproduction and photosynthesis.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A nuanced, non-obvious mechanism (sea rise as partial thermal buffer but net stressor) that complicates simple narratives about reef decline — useful for accurately modeling reef-dependent tourism and fisheries economies.
insights.locator: The effects of this are twofold

insights.claim: Modelling shows few coral reefs will retain the capacity to grow vertically fast enough to keep pace with sea level rise under a moderate-emissions scenario, despite some reefs currently managing to do so.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: A forward-looking warning that current reef resilience (vertical growth keeping pace) is not sustainable under moderate warming — signals accelerating reef loss ahead.
insights.locator: However, modelling has shown that few reefs

insights.claim: The world has lost nearly 10% of its coral cover since 1980 due to climate change-induced ocean warming, even as isolated cases like Sanya Bay in the South China Sea show sea level rise enabling recolonization of reefs dormant for over five millennia.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Net global coral loss (~10% since 1980) vastly outweighs rare localized recolonization gains, confirming the dominant trend is decline despite isolated positive exceptions.
insights.quote: But the opportunities for such recolonisation are far outstripped by the loss of coral elsewhere.
insights.locator: Sea level rise may also have the ability to spur reef growth

insights.claim: 49 UNESCO world heritage sites sit at low elevation along the Mediterranean coast, with 42 already facing erosion risk and 37 at risk from a 100-year flood event, both risks set to worsen through the century.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Nearly all mapped Mediterranean heritage sites already face active erosion or flood risk — a near-total exposure rate that should factor into heritage preservation funding and tourism-dependent local economies.
insights.locator: There are 49 Unesco world heritage sites

insights.claim: 3C of warming above pre-industrial temperatures would put nearly one-fifth of all UNESCO cultural world heritage sites at risk from sea level rise, including Japan's Hiroshima Peace Memorial, South Africa's Robben Island, Chile's Rapa Nui and the Sydney Opera House, with many becoming vulnerable at even lower warming levels.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Names specific globally iconic sites at risk, providing a tangible, high-visibility framing that could mobilize political and philanthropic capital for mitigation and heritage-preservation adaptation spend.
insights.locator: The sea level rise associated with warming of 3C

insights.claim: In Africa, 56 of 284 cultural and natural heritage sites already face flooding or erosion threats from sea level rise, a number expected to nearly triple to 191 sites by 2050 under a moderate-emissions scenario; mitigating emissions could cut very-highly-exposed sites by one-quarter.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Provides a rare quantified emissions-mitigation dividend (25% reduction in highest-exposure sites) that could be cited in cost-benefit cases for emissions policy tied to cultural preservation.
insights.locator: In Africa, 56 out of 284 cultural and natural heritage sites

insights.claim: Globally, 386 UNESCO heritage sites sit within 20 metres of sea level and are potentially affected by coastal erosion and flood hazards, comprising 289 cultural sites, 91 natural sites and six mixed sites.
insights.speaker: Giuliana Viglione
insights.so_what: Establishes the full global scope of heritage exposure as a discrete, countable inventory — useful baseline for insurance, preservation-fund allocation and cultural-tourism risk assessment.
insights.locator: Globally, there are 386 Unesco heritage sites
